title: Build your backend. Keep control.
text:
Build your backend. Keep control.

QB Flex gives your application a SQLite database, an authorized REST API, authentication, realtime events and object storage. Studio manages these services; your application connects through a publishable key and its own user sessions.

 Start here

1. Follow [installation](/docs/getting-started/installation).
2. Create your first project and an ownership policy.
3. Choose the [React tutorial](/docs/sdk/react/quickstart) or [Vanilla JavaScript tutorial](/docs/sdk/vanilla/quickstart).

 Three applications, one platform

Studio is the authenticated workspace for project developers. API owns management and application endpoints. Docs is this independently deployable documentation site. A background worker requests scheduled maintenance through an authenticated internal endpoint.

An organization owns projects. Each project owns an isolated primary branch. A branch has a separate SQLite file and authentication realm. Organization roles and application user identities are different permissions.

 What is available

The initial implementation covers ordinary-table REST CRUD, application policies, email/password authentication, database row subscriptions, basic S3 storage and backup/restore. Read the [compatibility reference](/docs/reference/compatibility) before deployment.

GraphQL, vector search, functions, hosted MCP, general branching and replicas are roadmap capabilities. They are not required to use the core backend.

 Secure by default

A publishable key identifies a project. It does not grant access to rows. Tables remain private until exposed, and exposed tables still need applicable permissive policies. Platform credentials never become application user sessions.

title: Install and run locally
text:
Install and run locally

 Requirements

Use Bun 1.4.2 and a running Docker-compatible engine for MinIO, Mailpit and container verification. Install the dependencies from the committed lockfile:


bun install --frozen-lockfile
cp .env.example .env
bun run dev


The development command starts Studio on port 7610, Docs on 7611 and API on 7612. All three applications have independent workspace commands. Database files and local secrets live under .data, which is ignored by Git.

The launcher checks for occupied ports before starting services and waits for the API to create and accept its worker credential. If the full Docker local profile already owns these ports, use its running applications or switch to native hot reload:


docker compose --profile local stop studio docs api worker
bun run dev


This preserves database and object volumes and leaves MinIO and Mailpit running. The native .data directory and the Docker database volume are separate installations. An independent worker must use the same QB_DATA_DIR as its API, or the same server-only QB_WORKER_TOKEN. The API owns credential creation; do not create or copy worker.token to bypass a startup error.

 Storage and email

Start the infrastructure services in another terminal:


docker compose --profile dependencies up -d --build


MinIO provides the S3 backend. Mailpit captures verification and password reset messages at port 7616. Configure the S3 environment settings in .env before starting the API. Local infrastructure credentials are development-only defaults.

 First owner

Open Studio. On a clean installation the setup screen asks for the bootstrap token, name, email, password and organization. The token is in .data/bootstrap.token; do not commit it. After successful setup the file is removed and the setup endpoint cannot create another owner.

Passwords must contain at least 12 characters. Sign in with the account you created. Production setup requires operator-supplied master and bootstrap keys.

 Verify your installation


bun run spike
bun run check
bun run build


The compatibility spike checks auth realm isolation and GraphQL interoperability. Native vector loading is reported separately. Passing local checks does not certify Linux deployment or remote OAuth providers.

title: Create your first project
text:
Create your first project

 Create a project

In Studio select your organization and create a project with a name and URL-safe slug. The initial region is local. Project creation returns an operation while the primary database is provisioned; Studio polls until the operation finishes.

Select the ready project. Its primary branch is shown with a production badge. Changes affect the selected branch.

 Create the task table

Use Database → Migrations to apply a migration:


CREATE TABLE tasks (
  id TEXT PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT (lower(hex(randomblob(16)))),
  owner_id TEXT NOT NULL,
  title TEXT NOT NULL,
  completed INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (completed IN (0, 1)),
  revision INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 1
);
CREATE INDEX tasks_owner_idx ON tasks(owner_id);


The schema is private at this point. In the exposure editor enable the table and allow its five columns, including the primary key.

 Add ownership policies

Create a policy for each of select, insert, update and delete, with the authenticated role and permissive mode. Both the read expression and write check use the same ownership condition:


{"op":"eq","left":{"column":"owner_id"},"right":{"claim":"sub"}}


This permits users to read and modify only their own tasks. An attempted ownership reassignment fails the write check and rolls back.

 Connect an application

Create a publishable key in API → Keys. Copy it when shown; only its hash and prefix are stored. Use the real project ID and primary branch alias in your client configuration. Run either example application with those values.

Sign up as an application user. This account is separate from your Studio owner. Insert a task with that user ID as owner_id, then open a second application account to confirm isolation.

 Generate types

The API workspace exposes generated types. The CLI writes the same declarations:


bun run qb types generate --project YOUR_PROJECT_ID --branch primary --output qb-flex.types.ts


Regenerate after schema changes. Runtime validation and authorization still apply to typed requests.

title: Build your first application
text:
Build your first application

 Prerequisites

Complete [installation](/docs/getting-started/installation) and [first project](/docs/getting-started/first-project). Create the tasks table with its generated ID, owner, title, completion flag and revision. Expose the columns and add owner checks for SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE. Create a publishable key.

 Choose a client track

Run bun run --cwd examples/react dev for the React application at port 7617, or bun run --cwd examples/vanilla dev for the DOM application at port 7618. Both implement the same workflow. Configure the API URL, project ID and publishable key in the form. Add that application's exact origin in Studio Authentication settings.

Follow the [React provider tutorial](/docs/sdk/react/quickstart) or [Vanilla JS tutorial](/docs/sdk/vanilla/quickstart). React uses a context provider, shared auth state and query/mutation hooks. Vanilla uses a client instance, DOM handlers and explicit cleanup.

 Register and create tasks

Register an application user with an email and a password of at least 12 characters. This account is separate from your Studio account. Add a task, mark it complete and delete it. The client sends the current user ID, and the API validates ownership independently.

Open a second browser profile with another application user. Each user should see only their own tasks. Attempting to update another user's ID returns a missing/invisible resource response.

 Receive changes

Both examples subscribe after loading a snapshot and its consistency token. Make a task change in another tab signed into the same user: the task list updates through committed, authorized events. Disconnect networking briefly, then restore it; the subscription resumes or requests a fresh snapshot when its retention window has expired.

 Add file attachments

Create a private bucket named attachments in Studio Storage. Enter its bucket ID in the example. Upload a file, download the exact bytes and delete it. Another user cannot list or download that private object. See [storage authorization](/docs/storage/files).

 Generate types and recover

Generate types in Studio API or with qb types generate. Create an encrypted backup, restore it into a separate branch and inspect the recovered task rows. Active sessions are excluded and object bytes need separate S3 backup. The primary branch changes only through an explicit cutover.

 Verify the workflow

The repository's browser checks run these workflows against the real API. Run QB_INTEGRATION_STORAGE=1 bun test tests/integration with the local MinIO dependency ready, then bun run test:browser. SDK packages are built and packed locally; no registry release is performed.

title: Use QB Flex Studio
text:
Use QB Flex Studio

 Project navigation

The persistent project and branch selectors define the target of each operation. Verify the environment label before SQL, policy changes or restore. Overview shows actual project state and recorded operations; it does not display simulated traffic.

 Database

Use the table list to select a schema object, inspect columns and view data. The grid requests bounded pages from the server. Filter and sort on the server, change visible columns, edit typed values and nulls, export the current page or import a JSON array of up to 100 rows atomically. Column controls affect the presentation; exposure settings define the public API. Studio data access uses organization permissions rather than an application identity.

The migration editor records a migration ID and SQL. Applied checksums are immutable. Use the policy editor and simulated identity tester to verify user-facing access.

 Authentication and API

Authentication lists application users and allows administrators to revoke sessions. Provider settings accept Google/GitHub credentials, exact origins and verification settings. Secret values are encrypted and never returned by configuration reads.

API shows endpoint paths, publishable keys and generated types. Use application credentials when testing public endpoints.

 Realtime and storage

Realtime documents subscription semantics and lets you inspect capability status. Use an actual application identity for event testing. Storage manages buckets and objects with upload, download and confirmed deletion. Studio uses audited organization capabilities; application uploads use the storage SDK and owner permissions.

 Logs, settings and recovery

Audit logs record actor, action and resource without credentials or row payloads. Settings expose organization and project configuration. Backups are created for the selected branch; restore creates another isolated branch before an explicit cutover.

 Unavailable services

Functions, AI, general branching and replicas are visibly marked planned. Empty screens explain availability without claiming that an operation succeeded.

title: Schema and migrations
text:
Schema and migrations

 Supported objects

The generated REST API supports ordinary tables with stable primary keys. Composite keys use a base64url-encoded JSON array in primary-key order. Views, virtual tables and custom-trigger tables are not automatically exposed.

SQLite remains the underlying SQL engine. Studio SQL is a privileged developer operation. Reserved _qb_ objects, extension loading, ATTACH and runtime PRAGMA changes are blocked through the console.

 Exposure

New tables are private. Exposure chooses the allowed public columns; all primary-key columns must be included. Policies are a separate requirement. Hiding a column rejects projections, sorting and filtering against that column.

 Migration lifecycle

Each migration records its identifier, checksum, author and application time. Reapplying the same identifier and content is idempotent. Changing the content of an applied migration returns a conflict.

Apply migrations under the branch owner transaction. Destructive migrations trigger a consistent backup first. Failed SQL or foreign-key validation rolls back the schema changes. Successful changes advance the schema version and regenerate managed event triggers.

Use forward migrations for corrections. There is no automatic destructive rollback. Restore a backup into an isolated branch when data recovery is necessary.

 Representation

Booleans use constrained 0/1 integers. Store dates as UTC ISO strings and JSON as validated text. Integers outside JavaScript's safe range are returned as strings. Write these values as signed 64-bit decimal strings. Blob writes and equality filters use canonical base64; JSON columns require valid JSON text. Blob values are base64 encoded in row responses and in authorized realtime projections.

 Generated types

Types describe the exposed schema, nullable values, defaults and generated columns. Simple CHECK (column IN (...)) constraints on literal values generate enum unions. More complex constraint expressions require explicit application validation. Insert fields with defaults are optional; generated fields are read-only. Keep declarations under version control and regenerate when migrations change.

 Out-of-band schema changes

The branch records a fingerprint of user tables, indexes, views and triggers. A schema changed through direct file access returns SCHEMA_STALE on public reads, mutations, schema discovery and row subscriptions. Reconcile it with a reviewed forward migration through Studio or CLI. Trusted file access still bypasses application row policies.

title: Write and test access policies
text:
Write and test access policies

 Policy model

QB Flex implements row policies in its application layer. Direct filesystem access to SQLite is trusted access and bypasses these checks. Policies are restricted JSON expressions rather than arbitrary SQL or JavaScript.

An operation needs at least one applicable permissive grant. Matching permissive expressions are ORed, and restrictive expressions are ANDed. No applicable grant means denial.

 Ownership example

For a table with owner_id, compare the column to the server-supplied authenticated subject:


{"op":"eq","left":{"column":"owner_id"},"right":{"claim":"sub"}}


Create separate select, insert, update and delete policies. Include authenticated in the role list. For inserts and updates use the ownership expression as the write check as well.

 Available expressions

Boolean expressions support and, or, not, true and false. Comparisons support eq, ne, lt, lte, gt, gte, in and isNull. Operands reference validated columns, verified sub/role claims or scalar values.

Relationship-existence expressions support {"op":"exists","relationship":"APPROVED_NAME","where":{"op":"true"}} for registered, exposed relationships. They apply the related table's select policies as well as the where expression. Unapproved relationships, cycles and excessive nesting are rejected. See [relationships and reviewed RPC](/docs/database/relationships-rpc) for setup and limits.

 Read and write semantics

Reads apply policies before counts and pagination. Updates check both the old row and the actual updated row; an ownership change cannot escape the new-row check. Atomic batches roll back if any prospective row is denied. Returned rows require select permission.

 Test identities

Use Studio's policy tester with a simulated user ID and application role. It executes the policy-filtered query without creating an unrestricted token. Then verify with real application users: two users should see separate rows, counts and realtime events.

 Realtime permissions

Events are reevaluated with current identity and policy. A deletion or row leaving visibility delivers only its key to an identity that could read the old image. A user who could not read that row receives no event.

title: Query the REST API
text:
Query the REST API

 Endpoints

The branch base URL is:


/v1/projects/{projectId}/branches/{branchId}


Use the primary alias or an explicit branch ID. Include X-QB-Key with a publishable key. Include an application bearer token when authenticated.

 Structured reads


{"columns":["id","title"],"filters":[{"column":"completed","op":"eq","value":0}],"order":[{"column":"id","direction":"asc"}],"limit":50,"count":true}


POST this body to /data/tasks/query. The default page is 50 rows; maximum is 500. Filters never accept raw SQL. Counts include only authorized rows.

 Pagination

Follow the response's meta.cursor with the same projection, filters, ordering, identity and schema version. Cursors are signed and bind that query scope. Changing scope rejects the cursor. Pagination does not provide a database snapshot spanning multiple requests.

 Writes

POST inserts one row or an atomic batch of up to 100 rows. PATCH updates a row by key; DELETE removes it. Supply Idempotency-Key to safely reconcile a retried mutation. Reusing the same key with different content returns a conflict.

Tables with a revision column support conditional updates through If-Match. The server increments revisions and rejects mismatched values.

 Results and errors

Success returns data and meta, including a request ID and relevant schema metadata. Errors provide a stable code, human-readable message and retryability. SDK methods throw QBError on failed responses.

An invisible row is returned as unavailable without revealing whether it exists. Public responses do not contain SQL, filesystem paths or credentials.

title: Relationships, upsert and reviewed RPC
text:
Relationships, upsert and reviewed RPC

 Register a relationship

Create a foreign key with a migration, expose both tables and the linking columns, then PUT a declaration to the branch Management API /relationships. Specify name, source, target, localColumn, foreignColumn and cardinality (one or many). A one relationship must follow a source foreign key. Reverse foreign-key links can use many.

A related query must select its linking column. Use .include([{ name: 'project' }]) after registering that relationship. Child rows pass their own SELECT policies; an invisible parent becomes null, and an invisible child collection becomes empty. Counts still describe authorized parent rows. Nested expansion is unavailable.

 Existence policies

A policy can use an expression with op: 'exists', a registered relationship name and a where expression evaluated against the target table. The target's SELECT policies are also enforced. This cannot turn a hidden table into a public join. Cycles and relationship paths deeper than four levels are rejected.

 Upsert

.upsert(row, { idempotencyKey }) requires every primary-key field. An absent row follows INSERT/WITH CHECK; a conflict follows old-row UPDATE/USING and new-row WITH CHECK. The entire batch rolls back if one row fails. It does not grant access to invisible conflicts. Returned rows must pass SELECT policies.

 Reviewed named operations

Developers register a declaration by PUT to /rpc in the branch Management API. A declaration contains name, table, kind, typed args, optional query settings, and value mappings. Mutation kinds are insert, update or delete; update/delete require keyArg. A value mapping can use { arg: 'title' } or { claim: 'sub' }. Claims come from the server identity.

The browser calls qb.rpc('operation_name', args, options). This API exposes structured operations over the same read/mutation engine. SQL text, arbitrary functions and unrestricted transactions are unavailable. Generated RPC declarations describe argument and return types. Pass both generated interfaces to createClientDatabase, RPC(options) to check operation names, arguments and results.

title: Authenticate application users
text:
Authenticate application users

 Separate realms

Platform sessions authorize Studio and management operations. Application users belong to a branch's authentication realm. Tokens from another project or branch are rejected, even when the same email address exists in both.

Better Auth provides password hashing, session creation, verification, reset and OAuth mechanisms. QB Flex provides routing, realm isolation and reserved metadata tables.

 Email and password

Use SDK auth.signUp, auth.signIn and auth.signOut. Passwords require at least 12 characters. Auth requests are rate limited. Revoking sessions in Studio takes effect on later requests and realtime authorization checks.

 Verification and reset

Enable email verification in project settings and configure SMTP. Unverified users cannot sign in when verification is required. SDK sendVerification requests a new message; resetPassword requests a reset link, and updatePassword completes it with the one-use token.

Use an allowlisted callback URL. Local messages appear in Mailpit. SMTP failures are recoverable operation failures rather than silently delivered messages.

 Google and GitHub

Register an OAuth application with the selected provider. Configure its callback to the explicit branch auth endpoint, then store its client ID and secret in project settings. Add the browser application origin to the project allowlist.

Call auth.signInWithProvider and navigate to the returned authorization URL. After the callback, refresh the application session. These adapters require provider credentials and live callback verification before certification.

 Browser sessions

The API uses HttpOnly cookies where supported, while SDK bearer tokens remain in memory. The client refreshes session state on initialization. Do not put service keys or management tokens in browser applications. Cross-origin cookies may be restricted by browser privacy settings; use a same-site deployment or explicitly manage an approved session adapter.

 Platform MFA

Platform owners can enable Better Auth two-factor authentication. Production readiness requires administrator enrollment and MFA enforcement; local availability alone is not a production certification.

title: Administrator MFA and recovery
text:
Administrator MFA and recovery

 Enroll the platform owner

Open Studio Settings even before creating a project. Enter the current password and enable the authenticator. Import the shown TOTP URI into an authenticator application, save the one-time recovery codes in a password manager and verify a code. The seed is shown during enrollment and never logged.

Production defaults to QB_REQUIRE_ADMIN_MFA=true. Owner and administrator writes require enrollment. Viewer access does not disclose secrets. Application user authentication is a separate branch realm.

 Sign in with MFA

After password verification, Studio shows the authenticator challenge. A password-only response does not contain an authenticated platform session. Enter a valid TOTP code to complete login. The Better Auth plugin applies attempt limits and locks repeated failed challenges.

Enrollment verification rotates the active session. Management tokens are revoked when enrolling; issue new project-scoped tokens after completing MFA. Keep recovery codes outside the data volume.

 Credential recovery

Use Better Auth's authenticated backup-code verification endpoint /platform/auth/two-factor/verify-backup-code when your authenticator is lost. Treat a recovery code like a password. An operator should revoke compromised management tokens and application sessions, rotate project keys and provider secrets, then examine audit events.

Never change the database's MFA columns to bypass a lost factor. Restore the protected control-plane backup only through an operator-reviewed recovery process.

title: Subscribe to row changes
text:
Subscribe to row changes

 Commit-driven events

Managed triggers write events in the same transaction as row changes. Rolled-back writes produce no events. Events have branch-local IDs, schema versions and insert/update/delete operations.


const channel = qb.channel({
  table: 'tasks',
  onEvent(event) { console.log(event.event, event.payload); },
  onStatus(status) { console.log(status); },
}).subscribe();
// When the screen is removed:
channel.unsubscribe();


 Snapshot and cursor

A query result contains meta.consistencyToken. Pass that value as the subscription cursor to receive changes committed after the snapshot boundary. Reconnect resumes from the last processed cursor and deduplicates event IDs.

Treat events as invalidation signals when maintaining a filtered/paginated list. Refetch the authorized query rather than assuming every update still belongs in your current list.

 Authorization

Join validates the publishable key, branch, session and exposed table. The connection rechecks authorization while delivering events. Session expiry, revocation or key removal closes the connection. Changes to identity reset the subscription.

Only authorized columns are delivered. Row removals deliver permitted keys. Do not treat realtime as a way around read policies.

 Delivery limits

The implementation provides single-node branch ordering and at-least-once replay. Frames are bounded to 64 KiB. Heartbeats keep connections active. Slow clients are disconnected rather than accumulating unlimited buffers.

Presence, broadcast, binary channels and multi-node fan-out are planned capabilities. Persistent application messages belong in ordinary authorized tables.

title: Upload and download files
Client SDKs
text:
Client SDKs

The two SDK packages share the same transport, authentication and authorization semantics. Choose the React package for component-level state and caching, or the framework-independent package for direct calls.

| Application | Packages | Guide |
| --- | --- | --- |
| React 19 | @qb-flex/client, @qb-flex/react | [React quickstart](/docs/sdk/react/quickstart) |
| Vanilla JavaScript | @qb-flex/client | [JavaScript quickstart](/docs/sdk/vanilla/quickstart) |

 Package availability

SDK artifacts are built and packed locally. They are not yet published to the npm registry. Workspace examples import the local packages. External applications can install the generated tarballs from dist/packages.


bun run sdk:pack


 Client configuration

Provide an API URL, project ID, branch alias/ID and publishable key. Set an exact application origin in project settings. Create one browser client for the application. SSR applications must create a separate client and query cache per request.

 Error handling

Methods return successful data envelopes and throw QBError for failures. Inspect its code, status and retryable fields. Validation, policy denials and conflicts should be corrected by the application; repeatedly retrying them does not help.

 Shared lifecycle

Subscriptions expose explicit cleanup. Session refresh is single-flight. Safe reads and explicitly idempotent writes receive bounded retries. Requests support timeout and AbortSignal cancellation.

React Native, offline writes, GraphQL, functions and AI SDK modules are deferred. Browser compatibility is the initial supported target.

Vanilla JavaScript quickstart
text:
Vanilla JavaScript quickstart

 Vite application

The runnable example is in examples/vanilla. It uses ordinary DOM APIs and no React dependency.


bun run --cwd examples/vanilla dev


Set the API URL, project ID and publishable key in the example configuration form. Add http://localhost:7618 to the project's exact origin allowlist.

 Import and initialize


import { createClient } from '@qb-flex/client';
const qb = createClient({
  url: 'http://localhost:7612',
  projectId: 'YOUR_PROJECT_ID',
  branch: 'primary',
  publishableKey: 'YOUR_PUBLISHABLE_KEY',
});


Install the locally packed client artifact when integrating into a separate Vite application.

First run bun run sdk:pack in QB Flex. In your Vite application, install the resulting tarball using its actual absolute path:


npm install /path/to/QBFlex/dist/packages/qb-flex-client-0.1.0.tgz


Import the client in your application entry module. The repository example already supplies a complete Vite configuration and can be copied as a starting application; its Vite version is pinned to 8.3.2.

 Direct browser modules

The Docs build includes a standalone browser ESM bundle at /sdk/client.js. Copy it into your application's public directory and import it locally:


script type="module"
  import { createClient } from '/sdk/client.js';
  const qb = createClient({
    url: 'http://localhost:7612',
    projectId: 'YOUR_PROJECT_ID',
    publishableKey: 'YOUR_PUBLISHABLE_KEY',
  });
/script


Serve the page over HTTP; do not open it through a filesystem URL. The standalone client bundle has no React or Node runtime dependency.

 Run the tutorial

Prepare the [task table and policies](/docs/getting-started/first-project), then add [authentication and CRUD](/docs/sdk/vanilla/data) and [realtime/file workflows](/docs/sdk/vanilla/realtime-storage).

title: JavaScript authentication and CRUD
JavaScript realtime and files
Use the qb CLI
text:
Use the qb CLI

 Login and linking


bun run qb login --url http://localhost:7612 --email owner@example.com
bun run qb projects list
bun run qb link --project YOUR_PROJECT_ID --branch primary


On macOS, login reads the password from a hidden interactive prompt and stores a 30-day management token in the OS keychain. Add --organization ORGANIZATION_ID only when the CLI must provision projects. Linux and CI use QB_MANAGEMENT_TOKEN: create the scoped token in Studio Settings after completing administrator MFA and inject it through your protected environment store. The CLI does not print or write credentials to a plaintext configuration file.

 Schema workflows


bun run qb db migrate --file migrations/001_tasks.sql --id 001_tasks
bun run qb db export --table tasks --output tasks.json
bun run qb db import --table tasks --file tasks.json
bun run qb types generate --output qb-flex.types.ts


Migrations and table writes require developer permissions. Import uses bounded batches; an import spanning batches is not a single all-or-nothing transaction.

 Recovery


bun run qb backup create
bun run qb backup restore --backup YOUR_BACKUP_ID


Restore creates a new isolated branch. It does not switch primary traffic automatically. Perform cutover deliberately through management operations after validating the restored branch.

 Development

qb init writes a local configuration file without credentials. qb dev starts the workspace processes. Commands accept explicit project/branch flags, with linked defaults for convenience.

General branch creation, functions, hosted MCP and remote reset are not enabled in P0. Unsupported commands return an actionable error rather than simulating success.

 Local reset and secrets

qb db reset --data-dir .data --confirm-local-reset requires a stopped API and a disposable local directory with a generated master key. It removes the local databases and generated local keys. It never selects a remote branch by default.

qb secrets set --name SERVICE_SECRET --env MY_SECRET reads a secret from the named environment variable, stores an encrypted version and returns only its identifier. Viewer access cannot recover secret values.

qb storage sync --bucket BUCKET_ID --directory ./attachments adds missing objects from a local directory. Existing and remote-only objects are preserved. Hidden files and symlinks are skipped. Use the explicit object APIs for deletion.

qb db diff --file expected-schema.json compares the current introspected schema with your checked-in schema manifest. It reports column differences; it does not invent a migration.

title: Deploy a single node
text:
Deploy a single node

 Deployment shape

The Compose deployment includes a gateway, Studio, Docs, API/database owners, maintenance worker and optional local MinIO/Mailpit. Keep writable SQLite files on persistent local storage owned by one API node. Never share a live WAL file across nodes or network filesystems.


docker compose -f compose.yml -f compose.selfhost.yml --profile selfhost build
docker compose -f compose.yml -f compose.selfhost.yml --profile selfhost up -d


 Required production configuration

Supply QB_MASTER_KEY, QB_BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN for the first owner, HTTPS QB_PUBLIC_URL, Studio/Docs URLs, exact allowed origins and S3/SMTP configuration. Use protected environment injection or mounted secret files rather than checking secrets into the repository.

The master key protects provider settings and backup encryption. Losing it prevents decrypting those records. Back it up separately and restrict access.

 Gateway and TLS

Terminate public HTTPS at the configured reverse proxy. Route API and Studio consistently so cookie and origin semantics match the configured URLs. Internal maintenance endpoints require the operator worker token. Do not expose MinIO operator credentials to browser applications.

Authentication rate limits use the API socket address, ignoring caller-supplied forwarding headers. Behind a proxy, clients therefore share that proxy's address bucket. Configure per-client abuse limits at the gateway; trusted forwarded-address processing is not implemented in this release.

 Docs publishing

Docs has independent build/start commands and prerendered HTML output. Set both QB_DOCS_URL and VITE_DOCS_URL before generating and building documentation to produce correct canonical and sitemap URLs. Host its static output separately or run its Bun server. No login is required to read documentation.

 Release verification

Local Linux builds, MinIO workflows and recovery drills are verified in the repository. Certify your production S3/SMTP services, live OAuth callbacks and load/recovery targets on the actual deployment. Check the implementation status before exposing a public service.

 Local object-store build

Historical MinIO container images are unavailable in the tested registries. infra/minio.Dockerfile builds the archived upstream community source at commit 7aac2a2c5b7c882e68c1ce017d8256be2feea27f and verifies its source archive SHA-256. The build preserves the upstream license. MinIO is a development backend; configure and certify your production S3 backend independently.

title: Backups and restore
text:
Backups and restore

 Consistent snapshots

Snapshots are created through the database owner using SQLite VACUUM INTO, then encrypted using AES-256-GCM and recorded with a checksum and schema version. Never copy only a live main SQLite file while committed changes remain in the WAL.

Manual snapshots are available in Studio and the CLI. The maintenance worker requests scheduled backups. Retention is configurable; the default is seven days.

 Isolated restore

Restore decrypts and verifies the checksum, writes a new branch database and runs integrity/foreign-key checks. Active sessions, verification challenges and stored OAuth access/refresh tokens are excluded. Restored application users remain in the isolated database and must establish new sessions.

Validate expected table data, policies and migrations before cutover. The restored branch has its own authentication identity and routing.

 Production cutover

The cutover endpoint requires the project owner role and an explicit project-slug confirmation. It creates a rollback backup, closes the old primary owner and changes the primary alias. Existing requests and sockets must be reconciled against the changed branch.

The previous primary is retired and refuses public reads and writes. Restore the rollback snapshot into another isolated branch to reverse the cutover. Do not assume that alias switching merges data.

 Object bytes and control metadata

Branch snapshots do not back up S3 object bytes. The worker separately creates encrypted, checksummed control catalog snapshots under backups/control with the same daily/weekly retention. Protect the master key and copy archives off the node; configure object-store versioning/backups separately.

Control recovery is offline. Stop the API/worker, preserve all referenced project database files and verify the archive before replacement. The local ownership lock prevents restoration over a running API. The command checks integrity, foreign keys, applied control migrations and referenced branch files, creates an encrypted rollback checkpoint, excludes platform sessions and revokes all restored project/management credentials. Reissue keys after recovery.


bun run qb backup control-create --data-dir .data
bun run qb backup control-restore --data-dir .data --file CONTROL_ARCHIVE --confirm-local-control-restore


Inject the original QB_MASTER_KEY for production recovery. A catalog archive does not include project databases or object bytes; coordinate their recovery to a compatible checkpoint.

 Recovery drill

Create representative data, take a snapshot, alter the data, restore into another branch and compare results. Repeat after a process restart and verify secrets/session behavior. Publish measured RPO/RTO only after a reference-dataset drill passes.

 Retention and cancellation

Maintenance keeps the daily window (QB_BACKUP_RETENTION_DAYS, default 7) and one newest checkpoint per week (QB_BACKUP_RETENTION_WEEKS, default 4). Preserve encrypted snapshots and the master key on separate storage for disaster recovery. A local backup volume is not off-site redundancy.

Project provisioning can be cancelled through POST /management/v1/operations/{id}/cancel while its status is requested. Running or completed operations return OPERATION_NOT_CANCELLABLE; cancellation never rolls back a committed database operation.

title: Monitoring and troubleshooting
text:
Monitoring and troubleshooting

 Health checks

/health indicates process liveness. /ready checks control-database access and reports active owner count. Readiness is not a claim that every external provider is healthy.

 Logs and audit records

Structured API errors include request ID, path, status and a stable code. Audit records include actor, organization/project, action and resource. Credential values, passwords and raw row payloads are not logged by default.

 Branch unavailable

Inspect provisioning status and confirm the persistent disk is mounted and writable. An unavailable or deadline-terminated owner returns a retriable failure. Restarting the API recovers branch handles; reconcile any uncertain mutation with its idempotency key.

 Busy writers and disk pressure

Requests are bounded by branch queue size and execution deadlines. Monitor database/WAL sizes and available disk. Stop introducing writes before the disk fills, drain work and follow the backup/restore runbook. Do not delete WAL files to reclaim space from a running database.

 Authentication failures

Verify project key, branch, exact browser origin and application session. A platform session cannot be used as an application identity. Check SMTP configuration for reset/verification delivery. Provider configuration alone does not prove a social callback works.

 Storage failures

Check S3 endpoint, credentials, physical bucket and bucket MIME/size constraints. Failed upload metadata is not publicly readable. Reconcile pending/deleting objects before retrying remote effects.

 Operational limits

This is a single-node implementation. Do not horizontally scale writable owners without fencing and routing certification. Advanced telemetry, distributed abuse controls and tenant fairness require the release tests listed in the development specification.

 Maintenance and metrics

apps/worker invokes the API's authenticated /internal/maintenance endpoint every minute. It removes expired sessions/idempotency entries, checkpoints WALs, retains the outbox for 24 hours, reconciles abandoned upload/deletion records and creates daily primary-branch snapshots. QB_BACKUP_RETENTION_DAYS defaults to seven. Local workers read .data/worker.token; production injects QB_WORKER_TOKEN.

Scrape /internal/metrics with the worker bearer token from the private network. The gateway returns 404 for internal routes. Prometheus output covers request/error counts, cumulative/max duration, active owners and available disk bytes. Do not interpret these as a complete tracing or performance certification.

Errors and limits
text:
Errors and limits

 Error contract

SDK methods throw QBError with code, message, status, retryable and optional details. API failures include a request ID. Preserve it when reporting a failure.

| Status | Meaning | Application response |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 400 | Validation or unsupported input | Correct the request |
| 401 | Missing, expired or wrong-realm credential | Authenticate again |
| 403 | Policy or organization denial | Check permissions |
| 404 | Missing or invisible resource | Treat as unavailable |
| 409 | Revision, checksum or idempotency conflict | Refetch/reconcile |
| 413 | Body or object size limit | Reduce the payload |
| 429 | Rate quota | Back off |
| 503 | Owner or external dependency unavailable | Retry eligible operations |

 Default bounds

Read pages default to 50 and cap at 500 rows. Atomic inserts cap at 100 rows. Query filters cap at 30, membership values at 100 and policy nesting at 12. Branch queues cap at 64 requests and active owners at 32 per API instance.

The default database and total reserved object quotas are 1 GiB per branch. Project configuration exposes quotas.databaseBytes, quotas.storageBytes and quotas.requestsPerMinute with optimistic If-Match updates. The default rate quota is 600 requests per minute per credential; the process keeps at most 10,000 credential buckets. Database admission includes the main file and WAL; a final admitted transaction may cross its threshold. Object intents reserve space before upload.

Realtime connections cap at 100 per project and 256 per process. Realtime frames cap at 64 KiB. Storage uploads cap at 100 MiB, with smaller bucket-specific limits. Privileged SQL console results cap at 500 rows.

Database pages and their expanded relationships share a conservative 2 MiB serialization budget, measured in SQLite before loading row values. Reduce the projection or page size after RESULT_TOO_LARGE. Events with oversized row images require a fresh snapshot instead of replay. The API admits four concurrent uploads and two snapshots; additional work receives retryable TRANSFER_BUSY or BACKUP_BUSY. Object listings currently return at most 500 ready objects.

 Safe retry

The SDK retries bounded safe reads and explicitly idempotent writes. A timeout may leave commit status uncertain. Reconcile using the same idempotency key; do not assume cancellation undoes a committed database transaction.

title: Compatibility and implementation status
text:
Compatibility and implementation status

 Verified locally

Bun 1.4.2, Elysia, worker-owned SQLite, Better Auth realm isolation, MFA enrollment/challenges, generated TypeScript, React Strict Mode lifecycle tests, realtime reconnect, MinIO storage and encrypted restore have executable tests in this repository. Consult VERIFICATION.md for the actual build/browser/Linux results and environment.

 Deployment certification

Google and GitHub adapters require your registered credentials and live callback testing. Production TLS, SMTP delivery outside Mailpit, encrypted disks, external S3 backends and sustained performance/recovery objectives require checks in your deployment. No scale, RPO or RTO targets are advertised as measured achievements.

 Measured baseline

On 6 October 2026, a Linux ARM64 container on an Apple M5 Pro host ran a one-million-row ownership-policy workload with WAL/FULL durability. With four CPU equivalents and an 8 GiB container memory limit, 1,000 indexed reads at 100 requests/second measured p95 4.29 ms; 100 writes at 25 writes/second measured p95 8.97 ms. All requests and authorized row events succeeded. Event delivery measured p95 250.18 ms from request start, including commit time. Snapshot and validated isolated restore took 1.393 and 1.820 seconds.

The temporary filesystem was Docker OverlayFS on the local VM disk. The shared VM reported 8,317,267,968 bytes of physical memory; the container's 8 GiB setting was a configured ceiling. These short virtualized runs do not certify sustained scale, multi-tenant fairness, power-loss recovery or production disks. [Download the raw result and environment metadata](/benchmark.json). The reproducible source is scripts/benchmark.ts in the repository.

 Native extensions

The macOS system SQLite rejects the tested dynamic vector extension. The bounded spike reports the result separately on each OS. Vector product features remain planned even when the Linux extension loads successfully.

 Current boundaries

Public APIs support ordinary tables, scalar filters, keyset pagination, atomic batches, upsert, registered foreign-key relationships, relationship existence policies and reviewed structured RPC. Relationship expansion is one level deep and capped at three relationships, 100 parent rows and 50 child rows. Policies reject recursive relationship cycles.

Storage has owner/private and public-read rules with bounded gateway uploads. Custom storage-policy expressions, resumable transfers and image processing are planned. Management tokens grant selected projects; server service keys require explicit branch/table/method scopes. SQL developer privileges are trusted schema administration.

The deployment owns all writable databases from one API process. It does not provide distributed owners, automatic failover, SQLCipher, point-in-time recovery or external OAuth certification. Metrics cover HTTP traffic, active owners and disk capacity; complete distributed tracing and advanced feature metrics are future work.

 Supported clients

The initial supported application tracks are React 19 and Vanilla JavaScript browser ESM. SSR must create a client and QueryClient per request; browser effects start after hydration. Other framework adapters and React Native remain deferred.

title: Complete development specification
text:
QB Flex — BaaS Platform Development Specification

Version: 1.0 • Date: 5 October 2026 • Status: proposed implementation baseline

 1. Product definition

QB Flex is a lightweight, self-hostable Backend as a Service for small applications, prototypes, internal tools, and early-stage products. It combines SQLite databases, generated APIs, authentication, realtime, storage, functions, and AI tooling behind a dark monochrome Studio.

The product should offer the convenience of Supabase while using Bun and SQLite as its core. It is a separate platform with its own APIs, SDK, CLI, and security semantics. Supabase interoperability is an explicitly scoped adapter project; neither its CLI nor its PostgreSQL wire protocol works automatically with QB Flex.

Primary goals: provision a project in minutes; create tables visually or through migrations; generate typed REST and GraphQL access; protect every user-facing data path; provide straightforward backups and local development; keep a single-node installation operationally small.

Initial scale assumptions: one writable SQLite database per project branch, local persistent SSD, one active database owner per branch, bounded write workloads, and one primary region. Higher traffic is addressed through independent project placement, read scaling, and quotas rather than simultaneous writers to one file.

Terminology: an organization owns projects; a project owns branches; each branch is an isolated database environment. Platform operators and project developers are control-plane identities. Application end users belong to a project authentication realm. A project role is not an application user role.

 1.1 Release scope

- P0 — foundation/MVP: organizations, projects, primary branches, SQLite lifecycle, migrations, table editor, generated REST, application RLS, email/password auth, initial social providers, realtime row events, basic S3 storage, TypeScript SDK, CLI, audit logs, backups.
- P1 — complete small-project BaaS: GraphQL, magic links/OTP, 20+ certified social connectors, phone auth, CAPTCHA, webhooks, presence/broadcast/binary channels, resumable uploads, image transforms, snapshot branching, AI inference/vector search, isolated Bun functions, hosted MCP.
- P2 — advanced platform: SSO, OAuth identity provider, read replicas, CDN integration, analytics buckets, RAG workflows, Deno functions, regional placement, Terraform provider, advanced Studio assistant.

These are delivery phases, not removal of requested scope. Feature flags and the Management API must expose availability and experimental status accurately.

 2. Feature coverage and SQLite adaptation

| Broadcast, presence, binary | Authorized WebSocket channels, heartbeat leases, bounded binary frames | P1 |
| Granular channels | Join/read/write/presence permissions, quotas, retention settings | P1 |
| S3-compatible storage | QB metadata/policies plus S3-compatible object backend | P0 |
| Global CDN | Optional CDN origin adapter; signed private access and public immutable caching | P2; requires CDN infrastructure |
| Image transformations | Isolated Sharp-based processing and derivative cache | P1 |
| Resumable uploads | tus-compatible gateway mapped to multipart object uploads | P1 |

| Inference, semantic search, RAG | Provider gateway, embedding collections, ingestion jobs and permission-aware retrieval | P1/P2 |
| Ollama, Llamafile | Operator-configured HTTP model adapters | P1; inference runs outside API process |
| OpenAI, LangChain | OpenAI provider adapter and documented LangChain integration | P1 |
| Global TypeScript/Deno functions | Region-pinned isolated Bun workers; optional separate Deno runtime | P1 Bun / P2 Deno; deployment infrastructure required |
| NPM modules | Build-time dependency resolution, lockfiles, runtime-specific compatibility checks | P1 |
| Region pinning | Project placement registry and regional worker routing | P2 |
| Built-in AI API | Unified inference, embeddings and retrieval routes | P1 |
| Supabase CLI | New qb CLI; migration guidance and optional import adapter | P0 CLI; not drop-in compatible |
| Management API | Versioned organization/project/configuration lifecycle API | P0 |
| Terraform provider | Provider over Management API, async operations and drift detection | P2 |
| MCP Server | Hosted Streamable HTTP MCP with scoped browser OAuth | P1 |
| Studio tabs | Database, Auth, APIs, Realtime, Storage, Functions, AI, Logs, Settings | Progressive across phases |

 3. Technical stack and responsibilities

| Layer | Technology | Responsibility |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Toolchain | Bun, TypeScript, Bun workspaces | Runtime, installation, scripts, builds and unit tests |
| Studio | TanStack Start | React application, routes, loaders and server rendering |

| Table UI | TanStack Table | Virtualized database grids, sorting, selection and column controls |
| Forms | TanStack Form | Schema-driven editors and validation |
| UI state | TanStack Store | Project/branch selection, panels and non-server transient state |
| Reactive collections | TanStack DB | Selected Studio collections and live derived queries; not the server database |
| API | Elysia | REST, authentication middleware, WebSocket gateway and management routes |
| GraphQL | GraphQL Yoga candidate mounted under Elysia | Generated schema, execution limits, resolver integration; validate Bun interoperability |
| Persistence | bun:sqlite | Prepared SQL, project databases and control-plane metadata |

| Telemetry | OpenTelemetry + structured logs | Request traces, metrics and job diagnostics |

Use pinned compatible versions and a committed Bun lockfile. Resolve exact releases during the initial compatibility spike; this document does not prescribe unverified future version numbers. Verify SSR, GraphQL, native extensions, auth adapters and image binaries together on the production Linux image.

TanStack DB is a client reactive collection layer. MVP uses Query for requests; DB collections are introduced only where live joins or optimistic interactions justify them. Cache ownership must be explicit so Query and DB do not independently mutate the same canonical collection.

UI reference libraries are optional copied/adapted components, not mandatory infrastructure dependencies. Confirm component licenses, accessibility, React compatibility, SSR behavior and bundle size before adoption. bklit.com could not be inspected during preparation; treat it as a requested design reference pending review.

 4. Architecture


flowchart TD
  Clients["Studio, SDK, CLI and AI clients"] -- Gateway["TLS gateway and project routing"]
  Gateway -- Control["Management API and platform auth"]
  Gateway -- Data["Project API, auth and realtime"]
  Control -- Catalog["Control SQLite and encrypted config"]
  Data -- Engine["Policy and query engine"]
  Engine -- Owner["Branch database owner"]
  Owner -- SQLite["Branch SQLite and transaction outbox"]
  SQLite -- Jobs["Durable job workers"]
  Data -- Storage["Storage policy gateway"]
  Storage -- Objects["S3 backend"]
  Jobs -- Extensions["Webhooks, AI and isolated functions"]


 4.1 Control plane

Manages organizations, memberships, projects, routing, region placement, branch lifecycle, keys, billing-ready quotas, operations and audit trails. Control-plane credentials never serve as end-user sessions. Initial deployment uses one control SQLite file with backups; an adapter boundary permits later migration if platform metadata concurrency outgrows SQLite.

 4.2 Data plane

Each branch has its own SQLite file and its own execution owner. API instances route work to that owner through internal authenticated IPC/RPC. MVP can colocate owner and API; production multi-node deployment must preserve ownership, fencing and authentication. Separate projects can live on different nodes.

Keep database handles in bounded worker processes or Bun workers. Synchronous SQLite execution must not block the shared API event loop. Use queue depth limits, query deadlines, cancellation/worker termination strategy, bounded result streaming and a capped connection cache. Confirm SQLite interrupt support in the selected runtime; if unavailable, terminate isolated query workers and recover safely.

 4.3 Deployment profiles

1. Local: one CLI-managed stack with Studio, API, worker and local S3 backend.
2. Single node: reverse proxy, Studio, API/database owner, jobs and persistent volumes; optional external SMTP, S3 and inference services.
3. Regional: control service plus region-specific owners, functions and storage adapters; each writable branch still has one primary.

Do not mount one WAL database across nodes or network filesystems. Durable local disks plus explicit replication/backup are required. Failover requires old-owner fencing before new-owner activation.

 5. Repository structure

  apps/
    studio/                  TanStack Start
    api/                     Elysia control/data endpoints
    worker/                  Durable jobs and outbox delivery
    function-runner/         Isolated function supervisor

    storage/                 S3/tus/transformation adapters

Packages import contracts rather than application internals. The policy/query engine is a single implementation shared by REST, GraphQL, vector retrieval and user-scoped function calls. Keep third-party providers behind interfaces.

 6. Database lifecycle and supported SQL

 6.1 File layout and settings

Use opaque server-generated IDs and canonical validated paths: /data/projects/project-id/branches/branch-id/main.sqlite. Never derive file paths directly from a user slug. Keep control data outside project files. Authentication and storage metadata use reserved _qb_ tables within the project branch where transactional coordination is needed.

Default connection initialization:


PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL;
PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;
PRAGMA synchronous = FULL;
PRAGMA busy_timeout = 5000;


Verify returned settings on every connection. FULL is the durable default; NORMAL may be an explicit operator tradeoff. Busy timeout is bounded waiting, not a throughput solution. Monitor checkpoints, WAL growth, free disk and long readers. Allocate per-project writer queues; expose saturation with a retriable error rather than unbounded waiting.

 6.2 Exposure contract

Introspect sqlite_schema, column/index/foreign-key PRAGMAs and migration records. Store exposure metadata separately from physical schema. Tables are private until deliberately exposed with policies. Public CRUD requires stable primary keys; define composite-key encoding. FTS/vector/virtual tables and views require explicit read adapters. Views are private by default because underlying row policies do not automatically apply. Arbitrary triggers, SQL console and migrations are trusted developer operations; they are not available to application users.

Represent booleans as validated 0/1, timestamps as UTC ISO strings or an explicitly selected integer convention, JSON as validated text and blobs as base64 or separate binary endpoints. Return 64-bit integers outside JavaScript's safe range as strings. Document nullability, defaults, generated columns and numeric precision in generated types.

 6.3 Migrations and schema cache

Each migration has ID, checksum, author, applied time, schema version and status. Reject edited applied checksums. Preflight SQL and backup before destructive changes. Apply migrations under an exclusive branch maintenance lock and a SQLite transaction where supported. Table-rebuild migrations copy, validate, swap and regenerate managed triggers atomically. No automatic destructive rollback; restore or apply a forward migration.

After commit, publish a monotonic schema version. Regenerate API metadata, GraphQL schema and type declarations; invalidate prepared statements and realtime/table caches. Requests carry or resolve a coherent schema version. DDL bypassing the migration API is detected and marks the schema stale until reconciled.

 7. Metadata model

IDs use opaque UUIDs; creation/update times use UTC. Foreign keys and uniqueness constraints are mandatory. Sensitive fields use encrypted envelopes referencing an operator-managed key; secret hashes are used where plaintext recovery is unnecessary.

 8. Identity, authorization and RLS

 8.1 Credential classes

- Platform session: Studio and organization administration, with owner/admin/developer/viewer roles.
- Publishable project key: identifies project; it does not grant unrestricted data access.
- End-user session/access token: project-bound user identity with validated issuer, audience, expiry and signing key.
- Secret service key: server-only explicitly scoped capability; bypass is opt-in, auditable and prohibited in browser bundles.
- Management token: granular project/org operations; never accepted as an application session.
- MCP OAuth token: tool scopes and selected projects; never inherits unlimited organization access.

Keys support rotation, expiry and revocation. Store hashes of opaque API keys, show plaintext once, rate-limit by credential and never log secrets. For browser sessions use HttpOnly, Secure cookies, controlled SameSite settings and CSRF protections. Bearer SDK sessions must have documented secure storage guidance. CORS origins and auth redirect URLs are per-project allowlists.

 8.2 Policy engine

SQLite does not provide PostgreSQL-style native RLS. QB Flex enforces policies at all exposed execution boundaries; trusted direct access to the database file bypasses this layer. Do not market file-level isolation as row authorization.

Policies use a restricted JSON AST, not arbitrary JavaScript or user SQL. Supported expressions include boolean operations, comparisons, null checks, membership and approved relationship existence checks. Claims are verified and server-supplied. Identifiers come from schema allowlists; all values use parameter bindings.

Policy combination rule: default deny; matching permissive policies are ORed, restrictive policies are ANDed, with at least one applicable permissive grant required. Roles are fixed by verified identity or trusted membership resolution.

- SELECT applies USING before filtering, joins, aggregation, counts and pagination.
- INSERT applies WITH CHECK to every prospective row after defaults and before commit.
- UPDATE requires old-row USING and new-row WITH CHECK; protect ownership/tenant columns against unauthorized reassignment.
- DELETE requires old-row USING; event delivery must not leak deleted row content.
- Upsert checks both insert and conflict-update paths. RETURNING obeys readable-column and row permissions.

Writes run inside one owner transaction so authorization and mutation cannot race. Privileged SQL-trigger behavior is treated as trusted schema logic; prevent triggers from rewriting protected values or validate actual final rows before commit. Gate unsupported trigger patterns on exposed tables. Public RPC is limited to reviewed named operations with declared policy context; never expose arbitrary SQL.

GraphQL relations, batched CRUD, realtime, storage, vector retrieval, functions and AI tools must use the same authorization model. Disable public aggregate capabilities that reveal inaccessible rows or hidden columns. A policy test UI evaluates fixtures under explicit simulated identities without minting unrestricted user tokens.

 9. Generated REST API

Base: /v1/projects/{projectId}/branches/{branchId}. SDK resolves a configured branch endpoint; production defaults to an explicit primary alias. No implicit branch from untrusted headers without validation.

| Route | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| GET /data/{table} | Authorized select, projection, filters, ordering and cursor |
| POST /data/{table} | Insert one or bounded batch; atomic by default |
| PATCH /data/{table}/{key} | Validated partial update, optional optimistic version check |
| DELETE /data/{table}/{key} | Authorized delete |
| POST /data/{table}/query | Structured advanced query AST |
| POST /rpc/{operation} | Explicitly registered operation |
| GET /schema | Public exposed metadata, excluding sensitive configuration |
| GET /openapi.json | Generated versioned API definition |

Filters: equality/inequality, ranges, null checks, bounded in, and approved text search. Relations come only from registry metadata. No raw SQL fragments. Identifiers are escaped after allowlist validation; values are parameterized. Default page 50, maximum 500, batch maximum 100 rows and configurable query complexity limits.

Use keyset pagination with a unique tiebreaker; opaque signed cursors bind filters, identity scope and schema version. Explicitly document that cursors do not establish a cross-request database snapshot. Offset pagination is optional for small Studio grids.

Success envelope: { data, meta: { requestId, schemaVersion, cursor, consistencyToken } }. Error envelope: { error: { code, message, details, requestId, retryable } }. Strip SQL, internal paths and secrets from public errors. Use 400 validation, 401 invalid identity, 403 denied operation, 404 missing/invisible resources, 409 conflict, 413 size, 429 quota and 503 owner unavailable. Avoid exposing whether a denied row exists.

Mutations accept idempotency keys scoped to credential, branch and operation; persist request hash and committed response in the same transaction. Reusing a key with different content returns 409. Conditional updates use an explicit revision column or server-managed revision rather than timestamp equality.

 10. Generated GraphQL API

Endpoint: POST /graphql. Generate types only for supported exposed objects. Use custom JSON, DateTime, Bytes and BigInt scalars; SQLite does not imply PostgreSQL GraphQL semantics. Generate paginated connections, allowlisted filter inputs and named mutations. Foreign-key relationships use batched resolvers and the shared policy engine.

Limits: maximum depth 8, configurable complexity budget, bounded aliases and page sizes, request/body/time limits, per-request DataLoader caches keyed by user and branch. Disable unrestricted introspection in production by configuration; developers can use authenticated schema tooling. Persisted operations are an optional production mode.

Schema changes are versioned; clients regenerate types on breaking changes. Realtime stays on the QB channel protocol initially. GraphQL subscriptions are a later transport adapter, not a second event source. REST and GraphQL must return equivalent authorized results for equivalent queries.

 11. Authentication

Integrate Better Auth through a project adapter only after proving database and cookie/session isolation. Use a separate platform realm and branch-aware application realm. Do not put all project end users in an unscoped shared auth table. External provider credentials and delivery keys are encrypted and bound to the realm.

Implement registration, email verification, login/logout, password reset, session listing/revocation, account linking and optional MFA. Use the library's reviewed password hashing, verification and session mechanisms; never implement custom cryptography. Token signing keys support kid, rotation and overlap. Project and branch audiences must be checked on every route.

Magic links and OTPs are single-use, hashed, short-lived and bound to intent. Set resend cooldowns, attempt limits and enumeration-resistant responses. SMS delivery requires an operator-configured provider and spending caps. Phone number changes require verification and sensitive-action reauthentication. Account linking requires verified provider identities and explicit confirmation; email equality alone is insufficient.

 11.1 Social provider acceptance registry

 12. Realtime and database change events

 12.1 Commit event source

Install managed INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE triggers on exposed ordinary tables to insert outbox events in the same SQLite transaction. Rollback removes events. Triggers capture primary keys and bounded permitted images; blobs/oversized columns are omitted or referenced. Outbox tables have no recursive capture triggers. Managed trigger regeneration is part of migrations.

Durable consumers poll committed events using a branch-local sequence. At-least-once delivery is expected; event IDs enable deduplication. Transaction IDs preserve grouping; order is defined within one branch, not across projects. Direct trusted SQL changes are captured only on tables with installed triggers. Changes on unsupported virtual tables require explicit adapter events.

This stream replaces the requested PostgreSQL listener for QB-native databases. A future external PostgreSQL connector can ingest logical changes, but is optional and not required to operate SQLite.

 12.2 WebSocket protocol

Endpoint /realtime; versioned envelopes include type, channel, ref, eventId and payload. Operations: join, leave, broadcast, presence-update, database-subscribe, ack and error. Reauthenticate on token refresh/expiry; reevaluate channel membership on revocation or policy changes.

Authorize database events under current identity and policy. Insert/update snapshots require readable new rows. Updates moving a row out of visibility may emit an authorized removal notification containing only previously authorized keys. Delete old images never go to users lacking permission. Replay uses current permissions and schema version; expired cursors return RESYNC_REQUIRED. Clients then query an authorized snapshot and resume with a server-issued cursor boundary to prevent missed changes.

Presence is ephemeral heartbeat state with per-connection IDs, user aggregation, TTL and disconnect grace. Broadcasting is ephemeral by default, acknowledged acceptance does not mean every subscriber received the message. Durable messages belong in application tables.

Default limits: 64 KiB event/frame, heartbeat 25 seconds, lease 75 seconds, 100 joined channels per connection and bounded outbound buffers. Binary frames have an authenticated/versioned header and obey the same channel checks. Slow clients are disconnected with resumable data-event cursors; binary broadcasts have no replay guarantee.

Multi-node fan-out requires an optional broker and shared presence coordination. Until that adapter exists, route branch channels to one realtime owner and advertise single-node semantics.

 13. Database webhooks and durable jobs

Create webhook subscriptions for tables and operations with reviewed payload projection. Queue deliveries only after transaction commit. Sign the exact body using HMAC with timestamp and event ID; publish receiver verification instructions. Support secret rotation with an overlap window.

Delivery policy: bounded exponential backoff with jitter, maximum 10 attempts over 24 hours, per-hook concurrency cap, timeout, dead-letter queue and manual replay. Receivers must deduplicate event IDs. Claim jobs atomically using leases, expire abandoned claims and record attempts. Jobs must be idempotent around external effects.

Block SSRF targets: loopback, link-local, metadata endpoints, private addresses by default, unsupported schemes and redirects to blocked destinations. Revalidate DNS and connection destination. Explicit operator allowlists enable internal targets when required. Redact request credentials and response secrets from logs.

 14. Storage, CDN and uploads

 14.1 Object contract

Buckets have public/private visibility, allowed MIME types, per-object size limits, retention and policies. Store object metadata in SQLite; bytes stay in S3. Object keys are project/branch scoped and normalized. Do not expose raw backend credentials. Authorized upload intents issue short-lived URLs limited to one object, size and content constraints supported by the backend.

Objects transition pending → uploading → verifying → ready or failed. Finalization checks backend existence, expected size/checksum and content validation before publishing metadata. SQLite and S3 are not one atomic transaction: use retryable workflows and orphan cleanup. Deletes use tombstones and retryable backend cleanup. Downloads require ready state and current policy.

 14.2 Resumable uploads

Expose tus-compatible creation, offset reads and chunk writes. Bind upload sessions to user/project/object, authenticate each request and expire abandoned sessions. Adapter maps chunks to S3 multipart uploads with backend minimum part sizes. Persist offsets only after bytes are durable; prevent concurrent offset races. Stream bodies with bounded memory and backpressure. Checksums, resume after restart and multipart abortion are release gates.

 14.3 Transformations and CDN

Transformation API allows bounded width/height, fit, quality and approved formats; rejects arbitrary commands and remote URLs. Detect dimensions before decoding, cap pixel count, strip metadata and use isolated workers with CPU/memory/time limits. Cache derivatives by source version plus canonical transform settings.

Public immutable objects can use long CDN TTLs. Private objects require edge token verification or short-lived signed access whose expiry governs cache behavior. Never share cached private content across users without authorization. Policy revocation and cache purge behavior must be documented; private authorization should be evaluated at delivery for immediate revocation.

Global CDN is an optional provider integration, not a property of SQLite or S3 compatibility. Show CDN provider status, region availability, cache hits and purge failures.

 14.4 Analytics buckets

Store append-only sanitized events as compressed partitioned objects with manifests. Aggregate usage in scheduled jobs into SQLite summaries for Studio. Optional columnar query adapter can be added later. Separate platform usage analytics from application events; define schemas, retention, consent configuration and project-specific access. Do not write sensitive row payloads into usage analytics.

 15. Backups, branches and replicas

 15.1 Backups and restore

Use a tested SQLite online backup or consistent snapshot mechanism, not copying only a live main file while WAL contains commits. Encrypt backup objects, checksum contents and persist schema/configuration manifests. Proposed defaults: daily full snapshots, 7 daily and 4 weekly copies; retention is operator-configurable.

Restore into a new isolated branch first, run integrity/foreign-key checks and compare expected migration/schema versions. Switching production traffic requires an explicit cutover operation, rollback checkpoint and old-owner fencing. Auth/session and secret restore behavior must be visible. Database snapshots do not restore object bytes unless object-version backups are enabled.

MVP recovery objective target: RPO 24 hours and RTO 60 minutes on the reference dataset, verified by drills. Continuous recoverable replication/backup is a P2 adapter with separately measured objectives. The API outbox alone is not sufficient for point-in-time recovery of every SQLite operation.

 15.2 Branching

Fork creates a consistent database snapshot, new identity/endpoints and independent policies/configuration. Default development branches exclude active sessions, production secrets, webhook destinations and scheduled jobs; auth users are excluded or explicitly sanitized. Storage metadata refers to immutable source objects read-only or copies selected objects through a declared operation. Branch writes always use a separate object prefix.

States: requested, snapshotting, validating, provisioning, ready, failed, deleting. Operations are idempotent and resumable. Branch TTL and disk quotas prevent forgotten copies. Promotion applies reviewed schema migrations to primary; it does not merge arbitrary divergent data. Offer schema diff/export; automatic bidirectional data merge is out of initial scope.

 15.3 Read replicas

P2 baseline replicas are asynchronously refreshed consistent snapshots, reporting applied generation and age. This provides read offload, not low-latency streaming replication. For incremental replicas, choose and certify an SQLite-specific replication engine before promising latency or automatic failover; do not manually copy live WAL files between running owners.

Clients choose primary or eventual; writes always route to primary. Read-after-write uses primary or waits for a verified consistency token within a timeout. If policy/auth/configuration freshness cannot be guaranteed, route protected reads to primary; stale replicas must not honor revoked access. Region placement and replica residency are explicit. Never allow a read replica to become writable without owner fencing and recovery validation.

 16. AI, vector toolkit and RAG

 16.1 Vector layer

Provide VectorAdapter operations for collection creation, upsert, delete and filtered nearest-neighbor query. sqlite-vec is a candidate requiring a Bun extension-loading, platform packaging and performance spike. Fallback exact search is allowed only for capped small collections and must be labeled. pgvector cannot run inside SQLite; an optional PostgreSQL adapter would be a separate backend.

Collections pin embedding provider/model/version, dimensions, distance metric and normalization. Enforce dimensions and reject mixed models. Index/version changes trigger re-embedding jobs. Store document metadata and ACLs alongside chunks; embeddings link to stable chunk IDs.

Permission filtering must occur before ranking/limit over unauthorized content, or use a bounded authorization-aware search strategy with correctness guarantees. Never fetch unrestricted chunks into a prompt and filter afterward. Delete/revocation must invalidate retrieval caches. Search returns source references, score and embedding version; thresholds are model-specific.

Assistant context includes selected schema, sanitized query errors and documentation. It may explain SQL, propose migrations, generate policies and diagnose validation errors. Show proposed diffs and affected resources before executing writes. Use user-scoped tools, current branch permissions and audit logs; never silently attach service keys.

Row values are excluded from AI requests unless explicitly included. Treat retrieved documents, SQL comments and tool results as untrusted instructions. Model output does not determine authorization. Destructive SQL, policy changes and production deploys require a visible deliberate execution action.  17. TypeScript and Deno functions

Deploy versioned TypeScript functions with HTTP and async-event triggers. Bun is the default; Deno runs through a separate optional runner. NPM support is evaluated per runtime and dependency; native addons and Node APIs are not universally portable.

Build pipeline: upload source → resolve locked dependencies → isolate build → scan/configuration checks → bundle → hash/store artifact → deploy immutable version → health check → switch alias. No dependency installation on an invocation path. Keep previous versions for rollback.

Run untrusted functions in per-project/version containers with unprivileged UID, read-only root, bounded CPU/memory/time/concurrency, no host filesystem or Docker socket, scoped secrets and controlled egress. A shared JavaScript isolate alone is not sufficient tenant security. For mutually untrusted public tenants, add a hardened sandbox/microVM boundary or keep hosting restricted until isolation is validated.

Proposed defaults: 10-second HTTP execution, 256 MiB memory, 1 MiB request, 5 MiB response and 10 concurrent invocations per project; async workloads use separate limits. Stream responses when supported and stop work on cancellation. User-invoked functions inherit user context by default; privileged service capability must be explicitly assigned and audited.

Region pinning binds function, project database and sensitive storage to permitted regions. Global invocation routes to the pinned region; it does not imply writable databases everywhere. External AI/email providers may process data elsewhere and must be displayed. Scheduled jobs use durable deduplication and at-least-once semantics.

Schema artifacts contain a hash/version. CI compares generated output with migration state.
